report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Humans have long tried to make artificial versions of our minds and bodies and other life forms.
Recent technological advances are poised to open Pandora's box and explore whether these artificial agents will become more human or alive.

In this paper we argue that this question needs to be addressed in tandem with the equally valid counterpart: to what extent do interactions with artificial others make humans less human and more artificial?
Living systems such as human organisms are fundamentally open systems, deeply connected with the natural world.
Yet, ubiquitous interactions with artificial agents from the cradle and across the lifespan may transform us, humans, into hybrid creatures.

It is not only the passive and rapid absorption of the increasingly complex cognitive content that matters, nor the mere sophistication of the conversational exchanges with AI agents or embodied interactions with robots.
Rather, the very nature of interaction itself matters too.
It's not what we learn, but how we learn and with whom we learn and what happens in between us and our creations.
The old Master Geppetto, so the story goes, was feeling lonely and thus he created a wooden, toddler-like puppet called Pinocchio.
After some magical interventions, the doll became alive and started to have his own agency, disobeying the old Master, creating serious troubles for both.
Humans have long tried to make artificial versions of themselves, creating animated machines that mimic biological motion and hence life -such as automata (Riskin 2003).
text.formatted: Humans have long tried to make artificial versions of themselves, creating animated machines that mimic biological motion and hence life -such as automata <ref type="bibr">(Riskin 2003)</ref>.

text.text: The newest and more sophisticated forms of machines, ranging from humanoid robots, to Virtual Reality (VR) characters to Artificial Intelligence (AI) powered agents, are likewise feared to develop their own agency, perhaps even consciousness and to "take over" and disobey their human makers the same way Pinocchio disobeyed the Old Master (Chalmers 2023).
text.formatted: The newest and more sophisticated forms of machines, ranging from humanoid robots, to Virtual Reality (VR) characters to Artificial Intelligence (AI) powered agents, are likewise feared to develop their own agency, perhaps even consciousness and to "take over" and disobey their human makers the same way Pinocchio disobeyed the Old Master <ref type="bibr">(Chalmers 2023)</ref>.

text.text: To what extent is this story just a science-fiction scenario or a feasible reality?

Given the unprecedented speed of technological advances claiming that at least some of these new artificial agents are poised to "come to life" and to display thereby their own forms of selfhood, embodiment and agency, this question is more pressing than ever.

Here we approach this question by focusing on two aspects: i) one emphasizing the tacit presence of the human in the making of artificial systems; and ii) one outlining the effects of interacting with artificial agents on human minds and bodies.
Consequently, two main claims will be made throughout the paper and will form a thread to guide our investigation.
First, we suggest that all artificial systems created by us, humans, biological life forms, are inherently hybrid by nature.
By this we mean that all artificial systems have the human mind in the loop either overtly or covertly.
We create artificial versions of our minds and bodies for various reasons but also to better understand ourselves.

This is why we start our paper with a discussion of human agency, selfhood, and embodiment before we set out to understanding selfhood, embodiment and agency in artificial and further in hybrid systems.

And this will be an important goal in our discussion -to outline the hidden variables in the equation which always lie within the tacit presence of Geppetto, the master, in the making of Pinocchio, the puppet.

Second, we suggest that the question whether interacting with artificial minds and bodies will eventually transform humans into more artificial-like, hybrid beings is the valid counterpart of the question whether artificial agents will become more human-like.
These two questions, we claim, need to be addressed in tandem because interaction is two-way.
Recent technological developments and studies show that humans promptly attribute human-like abilities to all sorts of human-made artificial agents (Ziemke 2023).
Less is known however of the effects of interacting with artificial others on the human mind, embodiment and sense of agency.

This is an important question because self-organising biological living systems such as human bodies are open, porous and vulnerable systems and hence constituted by the everchanging embodied interactions with the world and others (Varela and Maturana 1980).
text.formatted: This is an important question because self-organising biological living systems such as human bodies are open, porous and vulnerable systems and hence constituted by the everchanging embodied interactions with the world and others <ref type="bibr">(Varela and Maturana 1980)</ref>.

text.text: Humans are not solid immutable cement blocks, but rather open systems and dependent upon constant open bridges with the world.
Whatever system we interact with deeply impacts our psychological and embodied states.
Hence, we become not just what we eat, breath and consume, but also what we interact with, especially our technologies.
Humans are not just beings, but also "becomings".
The English language affords concision and clarity, capturing important and subtle distinctions.
For example, the word "being" can be used both as noun and a verb.
It is generally admitted that human organisms are beings, i.e. spatiotemporally instantiated existing entities.
The problem here is that one may conceive beings as reified solid objects, more like chairs rather than clouds.
When we say that humans are "becomings" rather than beings, the aim is to outline the inherent transformatory and dynamic process that constitutes human existence (Noë 2004).
text.formatted: When we say that humans are "becomings" rather than beings, the aim is to outline the inherent transformatory and dynamic process that constitutes human existence <ref type="bibr">(Noë 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Our interactive experiences with the world and others constantly modify our inner life and embodiment for the better and for the worse: whether, when we cry as a baby, we are faced with a smile or with hostility will deeply modify our neurobiology and stress response.
Persistent or repeated experiences like that can have effects across the lifespan.
As we will see shortly, agents act and interact with the world constantly.

By definition, interactions are always bidirectional and humans, understood from the developmental perspective, are malleable, vulnerable and constantly influenced by interactions with the world and others.

It is thus important to keep in mind i) what type of artificial and biological systems we interact with on daily basis, and ii) what type of interactions these artificial agents afford and their effects on our human minds.
Humans are great imitators and we swiftly copy those who surround us.
To quote the timeless wisdom of Aristotle passed on by our grandmothers: "be careful with whom you hang out, as you will become more like them unwillingly!".
This paper addresses the following three intertwined questions.
What is an agent and what is agency in biological and artificial systems?

(Section 2) ii) What type of artificial versions of the human-like psychological and embodied abilities are currently implemented in the field as autonomous agents that may take over and develop their own "mind"
and agency?
(Section 3 &4) iii) And finally, what are the consequences for human minds and bodies of interacting with artificial minds and bodies in our daily lives?
text.formatted: (Section 3 &4) iii) And finally, what are the consequences for human minds and bodies of interacting with artificial minds and bodies in our daily lives?

text.text: (Section 5)

In addressing this last question, we will explicitly endorse a developmental perspective because, unlike artificial agents, human bodies and minds grow and develop necessarily in relation to other minds and bodies (Ciaunica 2017).
When it comes to understanding the human mind, the infant is, to use Wordsworth's famous metaphor, "father to the (hu)man".
A robust body of evidence suggests that infants have much more sophisticated socialcognitive skills than previously suspected.

The issue at stake is crucial since as Woodward and colleagues (2001) pointed out, assessing infants' understanding of others' behaviour provides not only a snapshot of the developing mind of the child, but also insights into the very nature of cognition itself.
text.formatted: The issue at stake is crucial since as <ref type="bibr">Woodward and colleagues (2001)</ref> pointed out, assessing infants' understanding of others' behaviour provides not only a snapshot of the developing mind of the child, but also insights into the very nature of cognition itself.

text.text: But first, we review some working definitions of the key concepts of self, body, agent and agency in biological systems with a focus on humans.
Why start with biological systems?
Because without Geppetto, no Pinocchio.
Who is Geppetto?
Humans are self-organising biological systems that make artificial versions of themselves by modelling their own cognitive and/or embodied abilities.
Making an artificial version of oneself may be thus added to the list of abilities that sets humans apart from other living beings in the animal world.
But above all, Geppetto is an agent with a sense of control over his actions: for example, one day he wakes up and decides to make a toddler-puppet, instead of making a chair.
The term "agent" has its origins in the Latin "agere" which roughly means "doing".
In this minimal approach, agents are entities that do stuff in the world.
This definition however is too loose to bear any meaningful significance, hence one needs to refine it by inserting additional constraints.
For example, an agent can be defined as an entity that acts in the world with a goal.

This extra constraint introduces the critical feature of goaldirectedness (which some artificial agents may possess, e.g., the robot Roomba acts in the world to achieve the goal of cleaning my living room).

Yet, one may argue that goal-directedness is not sufficient for agency: for example, I may have the intention or make a choice to clear or not to clean my living room, while Roomba doesn't: once I hit the button, the robot must follow the received instructions.
Intentionality thus -not to be conflated with goal-directedness -may be considered a core part of what it means to be an agent and hence to have agency.

Furthermore, to be agentic, an entity not only acts but importantly also flexibly inter-acts with the world and is capable of adjusting her goals and behaviours as a function of the outcomes of the interaction itself and the goals and behaviours of other agents in the environment.

An agent thus is typically defined as a system or entity that willingly and directly interacts with its surroundings through its physical embodiment to perform tasks and achieve goals (Gallagher 2020).
Goals can be individual or collective or a combination of both.
The tasks can be internally or externally driven.
This is a distinction that can help show the difference between natural and artificial agents.
For example, living systems or agents have the internal, intrinsic goal of looking for food and avoiding harm.
When I was born, I did not choose to be hungry and hence to look for food.
The goal of staying alive is inherently built-into my biophysiological make up.
By contrast, artificially made systems or agents such as the robot Roomba have the externally driven goal of cleaning the room -without any care or concerns about harming or nurturing itself.
The job the robotic system is doing has no bearing upon its ontological existence and it doesn't participate actively in its own creation.
In short: if I don't eat, I will cease to exist.
If my Roomba stops cleaning the room, it doesn't stop existing.
As we will see shortly, this observation will be important in the distinction between biological and artificial agency and embodiment as defined by pioneers such as Maturana and Varela (1980).
text.formatted: As we will see shortly, this observation will be important in the distinction between biological and artificial agency and embodiment as defined by pioneers such as <ref type="bibr">Maturana and Varela (1980)</ref>.

text.text: Although there is some debate about the extent to which the ability of a biological or artificial system to have agency is related to the ability of that system to display self-organising or self-preservation behaviour (Ciaunica 2025), we think the notion of self (and self-organization) is intimately connected to the notion of agency.

In this view, to be truly an agent with agency, means not only to act and interact with the world, but importantly to do so in order to sub-serve the fundamental goal of the system's self-preservation.
As Jonas (1966) puts it, "this world is at once inviting and threatening."

Biological organisms continuously construct and maintain themselves against the natural tendency toward dissolution and decay (Lyon 2006) and they do so by acting in the world as animated agents modifying their inner states, their behaviour and the world.

Some authors have argued that the concept of agency is crucially complemented by the concept of "sense of agency", which refers to the experience of being the initiator of one's own voluntary actions and through them influencing the external world (Haggard 2017; Beck et al., 2017; Hommel, 2017; Cornelio et al. 2022).
text.formatted: Some authors have argued that the concept of agency is crucially complemented by the concept of "sense of agency", which refers to the experience of being the initiator of one's own voluntary actions and through them influencing the external world (Haggard 2017; <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Beck et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Hommel, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Cornelio et al. 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The subjective feeling of being in control of one's actions is thus considered a key indicator of whether a system is truly agentic or merely does stuff in the world by obeying certain rules or set of instructions, like a Roomba or a thermostat.
On this view, the sense of agency refers to the capacity to experience goal-directed motor actsmoving the body with intentional control to achieve a goal.
In this respect the sense of agency has been defined as the experience that links intentions to their external consequences.
For example, the match between the intended and actual outcome of an action produces a feeling of being in control (Synofzik et al., 2013).
text.formatted: For example, the match between the intended and actual outcome of an action produces a feeling of being in control <ref type="bibr">(Synofzik et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: The brain mechanisms underlying this embodied and agentic experience are quite efficient and well known, acquired very early in development.
Evidence of early sense of agency in infants as young as 2 months of age has been demonstrated for some basic bodily actions such as smiling and thumb sucking (Rochat and Striano, 2000).
text.formatted: Evidence of early sense of agency in infants as young as 2 months of age has been demonstrated for some basic bodily actions such as smiling and thumb sucking <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Rochat and Striano, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Later in development, we start to use our bodies to control the external world, with evidence showing that we promptly extend our sense of agency through the objects (tools) we interact with (Iriki et al., 1996 (Iriki et al., , 2001)).
text.formatted: Later in development, we start to use our bodies to control the external world, with evidence showing that we promptly extend our sense of agency through the objects (tools) we interact with <ref type="bibr">(Iriki et al., 1996</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Iriki et al., , 2001))</ref>.

text.text: It has thus been proposed that the sense of agency includes at least two aspects, body agency (the motor control aspect) and external agency (the intentional aspect of accomplishing a goal) (Wen, 2019; see Gallagher 2012).
Body agency refers to the experience of controlling one's own body and receiving the bodily feedback that results from the bodily movement one initiated voluntarily (e.g., moving my hand).
External agency refers to the experience of acting to voluntarily control external events and obtaining the corresponding and matching external feedback from the objects in the world.
The action-effect causality is key for our interactions with AI, VR and robotic technologies (see also Kagan, this issue).
More generally, and in the first place, for an entity to have a sense of agency requires that it have the capacity to experience something (Gallagher 2000 , Damasio 2000).
text.formatted: More generally, and in the first place, for an entity to have a sense of agency requires that it have the capacity to experience something <ref type="bibr">(Gallagher 2000</ref> <ref type="bibr">, Damasio 2000)</ref>.

text.text: One influential view in philosophy of mind and cognition stipulates that for the human and for some non-human animals prereflective bodily experiences anchor the first- Human agents thus have the property of embodied (as-subject) selfhood (Damasio 2000; Ciaunica 2025).

1 Even neonates are self-aware in this minimal prereflective sense, even though they can't recognize themselves in a 1 Damasio has developed a multilayered approach to self-processes, from protoself to core self to autobiographical self, with each advancing stage explained by specific brain-body architectures and the processes they execute (Damasio 2018).
See Prescott et al. 2024 for an opposing view.
mirror (Rochat 2019).
text.formatted: mirror <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Rochat 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, an important part of the prereflective sense of agency involves a basic differentiation between self and non-self, where non-self includes other agents.

This experiential requirement is currently debated by researchers who question whether without it basic biological systems such as cells, and artificial systems such as AI and robots, and bio-synthetic machines are truly agents.
The question of whether a cell or an artificial system "feels in control" over actions in the world is beyond the scope of this paper and its current focus.
2 However, to say that the sense of agency is complementary to, or a key indicator of agency is not to say that it is constitutive of agency.
Even if human agency generally involves having a sense of agency (something that may be disrupted in specific pathologies), it does not mean that there can't be agency without it.

3 For example, robots that are able to self-recognize as the object in a mirror are not self-aware as subject, because they lack an inherent first-personal embodied subjectivity, which is to say, they lack consciousness Robots, however, are able to non-consciously register themselves as an object of their perception and therefore register the difference between self and non-self.

Georgieff and Jeannerod (1998), for example, provided a neuroscientific (sub-personal) account of this differentiation in terms of a "who" system (a comparator) in the human brain that permits the identification of onself as the agent of an action and thus non-consciously differentiates the self from external agents.
This type of comparator mechanism has been engineered in some robotic designs (Pitti et al. 2009).
text.formatted: This type of comparator mechanism has been engineered in some robotic designs <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Pitti et al. 2009</ref>).

text.text: An artificial agent clearly is not equivalent to a natural (biological) agent.
It may lack a sense of agency, and it may lack any display self-organising or self-preservation behaviour.
A robotic agent, however, can interact with its surroundings through its physical embodiment to perform tasks and achieve goals, and it can differentiate itself from what is not itself.
It can be agentive object even if not fully a subjective agent.
3 Learning from the Mind -making neuro-inspired artificial agents
It is the human mind and not the body that was first in the spotlight in the contemporary race of making artificial versions of ourselves.

By creating artificial systems with focus on what makes humans "special" (i.e., the mind, or cognitive brain power), the tacit hope was to capture the very essence of what makes us humans, what set us apart from other biological organisms say.
Building artificial smart agents took early inspiration from the human brain and its complex neural architectures.
The first pioneering attempts to build artificial minds focused on the computing power of the human brain (Anderson et al. 1993).
text.formatted: The first pioneering attempts to build artificial minds focused on the computing power of the human brain <ref type="bibr">(Anderson et al. 1993</ref>).

text.text: The idea of artificial neural networks builds on early models of sensory processing by the brain (Krogh 2008).
text.formatted: The idea of artificial neural networks builds on early models of sensory processing by the brain <ref type="bibr">(Krogh 2008</ref>).

text.text: An artificial neural network is typically created by simulating a network of model neurons in a computer (Minsky & Papert 2017).

text.text: Computational models and studies of homeostasis and the brain can be traced back to the era of cybernetics.

In the field of dynamical systems theory, Ashby's famous homeostat coupled electrical and magnetic sensors and effectors such that when perturbed it executed a random parameter search until equilibrium was restored (Cariani 2009).

text.text: One influential proposal to couple brain, body and environment is Karl Friston's Free Energy Principle (FEP henceforth).

According to FEP, any self-organising system such as the human body has to resist the natural tendency to disorder (implied by the second law of thermodynamics) in order to maintain their states and form in the face of a constantly changing environment.
Self-organising organisms complete this task through the dynamic updating of Bayesian sensory predictions.

On this view the brain is thus processing dynamically shifting generative models of what is causing incoming sensory events, based on probabilistic predictions about how likely something is to have happened and what the likely causes are.
This approach relies heavily on the capacity of the organism to engage in action in the world in order to "fulfil" its predictions and maintain inner states within a viable range for survival.

Indeed, it has been recently suggested that the basic prereflective experience of being a self is the result of an ongoing predictive coding (PC) process within a generative model that is centered on the organism (Friston 2010; Clark 2013).
On this view, the self is thus a result of dynamic self-modelling mechanisms.

However smart, creating a soft body does not intrinsically solve the "self-care" problem, or how to maintain homeostatic self-regulation within viable constraints.
The vulnerability inherent to the softness of the body is not related to the degree of "fragility" of the material that makes the body.
Rather the vulnerability of the living body is related to the vulnerability inherent to the openness and sharedness that characterize the living organisms related to their world.
Living systems are not vulnerable because they are soft; organisms are vulnerable because they care about themselves and their connections to the world and others.

Rapid technological advances promise that our future daily lives will be richly populated with artificial Pinocchios autonomously acting in the world, out-and-about and bursting with superhuman energy and performing actions drastically more sophisticated than the modest cleaning Roomba.
Creating artificial agents per se is an interesting endeavour, yet interacting with them is perhaps the most important part of the journey.
After all, Geppetto made Pinocchio to palliate his loneliness and for company.
The interactive social aspect is a fundamental component in making artificial agents.
Interactions with artificial agents are poised to become ubiquitous in our modern world, occurring very early in development and stretching across the lifespan.
Now, one may wonder whether AI systems or biorobots will become at some point soon conscious agents, and having experiences.
This question is currently heatedly debated in the field (Chalmers 2023) and lies beyond our scope here.
Rather we propose to turn the investigatory lens / telescope around towards the human side of the equation.
Let's have a closer look at us, humans, the mysterious makers of Pinocchio AIs and robots.
What type of hybrid agencies are we co-constructing in our daily interactions with these new types of minds and bodies?
What is the effect of interacting with artificial minds and bodies on the human mind and body?
By interacting with artificial others, will these artificial agents become more like us, or us like them?
Or both?
And if the future is entirely hybrid, to what extent will the boundary between biological and artificial life become indistinguishable?
As we mentioned in the Introduction, two claims are proposed here which need to be considered necessarily in tandem, as two faces of the same coin.
First, all artificial agents are in a fundamental sense hybrid because they are made by us, humans (i.e. biological systems).

By being an extension of our cognitive and embodied capacities, all artificial minds and bodies contain tacitly, at their very core, the biomimetic design principles that human agents used to implement at various levels within the AI and (bio)robotic architectures.
This claim states basically that artificial agents do not burst into existence magically, as external creatures independent of the human mind.
We don't wake up in the morning to find computers or LLMs in a forest the same way we find microbes under the microscope.
Human thinkers had to work hard to test and implement the best principles to make these artificial agents pop into existence.
To use a metaphor: consider an archer sending an arrow.
Once the arrow is released towards its target and flies in the air, one may be tempted to forget about the archer and the bow she used to send the arrow out there in the world.

Yet, no matter how sophisticated the artificial arrows our technologies will produce, no matter how far they will reach, and no matter how autonomously they will adapt to hit their targets,foot_0 the archer's cognitive and embodied make-up remains a constitutive part of the entire trajectory, and it would be a mistake to ignore it.

text.text: The second important claim here is that interacting with artificial agents will ultimately change our minds and bodies deeply, transforming us into hybrid creatures.
Hence the question whether AIs and (bio)robots will gradually become more human needs to be addressed in tandem with the equally valid counterpart.
Aren't we humans, going to become more artificial as we gradually replace our daily human-to-human interactions with artificial others?
Why is this important?
Because living systems such as human organisms are not fixed entities nor set in stone, but rather porous, vulnerable and flexible systems.
Human agents are deeply and sometimes irreversibly transformed by the machines they interact with, regardless of whether the latter are perceived as being experiential, conscious agents.

For example, in the 1936 classic film "Modern Times" featuring the famous Charlie Chaplin actor one can see how the agentic behaviour of the main character is transformed by the interactions with the gears and mechanisms of the machine.
Yet, no debates were held in 1936 around gear/machine consciousness.

The important aspect here is to keep the focus on how the human side of the agentic equation is affected by interactions with a machine or artificial agent, especially in early development and on regular basis across the lifespan.
This is currently an open question which needs to be addressed systematically and rigorously at both theoretical and empirical levels.
As we saw earlier, living systems such as human organisms are fundamentally open systems, continuously shaped and constituted by exchanges and interactions with the external world.
What is the effect of interacting with artificial agents (embodied or disembodied) on the human sense of self and agency?
After all, Geppetto created Pinocchio because he wanted to feel better and less lonely, and not as some maladaptive self-defeating behaviour.

After all, the real challenge for AI designers, industry and engineers is to make a puppet Pinocchio acting autonomously in the world, while Geppetto relaxes and drinks a coffee.
But an even more important achievement would be to create artificial agents that complement human agency -systems that can work with Geppetto rather than instead of him.
To achieve this task, it should be apparent that focusing on cognitive abilities and neural networks is not enough.
One has to consider the body and its constant interactions with the environment.
Indeed, the propensity to analyze minds based on purely abstract models unrelated to the life of the body, of the social/physical environment, has been vigorously challenged.
To construct artificial others, one has thus to start with the developing body, with focus on its self-preservation mechanisms.
Importantly and perhaps paradoxically, autonomous and adaptive interactions with an unpredictable world necessarily depend on the degree of openness and sharedness to the world and others.

In this paper we argued that the question of how to make artificial systems more human-like needs to be addressed in tandem, as two sides of the same coin, with the question: to what extent do interactions with artificial others make humans less human and more artificial?

We built upon the observation that the distinction between mind and body permeates the modern history of thought and by extension the creation of artificial systems that think and perform actions like us in the world.
Humans build artificial minds and bodies by taking as inspirational muse their own minds and bodies.
Hence, in this sense, all human-initiated and human-made artificial systems are hybrid systems and thus hybrid agents, precisely because they depend upon humans for their ontological existence.

Pinocchio may disobey and "act out" capriciously by following his own mind and agency, yet Geppettolike abilities may still partly and tacitly be present in Pinocchio in the form of underlying ontology and cognitive make up.
Perhaps more importantly, we also argued that we ourselves become hybrid through our interactions with our artificial creations.
Indeed, it is not only the passive absorption of the cognitive content that matters, nor the mere sophistication of the conversational exchanges with AI agents or embodied interactions with robots.
The very nature of interaction itself matters too, which highly depends on the development and the situated embodiment of the co-actors (human or artificial).
